Write an email to a colleague about the anniversary of a public website your team runs. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: Five years of the service, and what comes next

Hi Sam,

Next Tuesday marks five years since we put the public site live, and I wanted to say a few words before the date slips past us.

When we launched, the idea was simple: one place where people could find what they need without first having to work out which part of the organisation to ask. It was smaller then. A few hundred pages, a search box that wasn't very good, and a team of six who were still arguing about the colour of the buttons. Today it serves more than two million visits a month, and most of those people get what they came for in under a minute. That is what we set out to do, and I think we should say so plainly.

Let me be clear about what has made the difference. It isn't any one piece of technology. It's that we kept listening to users, shipped small changes often, and fixed things in the open when they went wrong. The move to cloud hosting in year two, the rewrite of the guidance pages after the accessibility audit, and the new search last spring all came from the same habit: look at what people actually do, then change the thing.

I'd like us to mark the anniversary without making a fuss. Three suggestions:

1. A short post on the team blog, written by the people who did the work rather than by me. I'd love you to draft the section on the search rebuild.
2. A look back at the numbers: traffic, satisfaction, cost per visit. Priya has most of this already, and I've asked her to pull it together by Friday.
3. An hour together on Thursday afternoon, with cake, for everyone who has worked on the site over the years, including those who have moved on to other teams.

The most important thing we should take from five years? A live service is never finished. The content is still too dense in places, the mobile experience can be better, and we have more to do on plain language. I'd rather use the anniversary to agree our priorities for the next twelve months than to congratulate ourselves for too long.

Could you let me know by Wednesday whether the blog post is something you can take on? If the timing is a problem, don't hesitate to say so, and we'll find another way.

Thank you for everything you've done to get us here. It's been a pleasure to watch it grow.

Best wishes,
[name]
